title: Objects, References and Copying Multiple Choice
description: Reference vs value, shallow/deep copy, structuredClone, and Object.hasOwn from module 02.

questions.explanation: `b = a` copies the reference, not the object. Both variables point to the same object in memory, so mutating through `b` is visible through `a`.
The spread operator only shallow-copies top-level keys. `copy.profile` still references the same nested object as `original.profile`, so mutating it affects both.

questions.prompt: Which built-in creates a true **deep clone** and preserves types like `Date`, unlike `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value))`?
questions.explanation: `structuredClone` recursively clones nested structures and preserves types such as `Date`, `Map`, and `Set`. `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...))` loses `Date` (converts to string) and drops `undefined`/functions. `Object.assign` and spread are only shallow.

questions.prompt: What happens to a `Date` value after `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({ when: new Date() }))`?
questions.explanation: `JSON.stringify` serializes `Date` objects via `toISOString()`, producing a string. Parsing that JSON back does not restore the `Date` type — this is a common lossy deep-copy pitfall.

questions.prompt: Given `const user = Object.create({ role: "guest" }); user.name = "Ana";`, what does `Object.hasOwn(user, "role")` return?
questions.explanation: `role` lives on the prototype passed to `Object.create`, not as an own property of `user`. `Object.hasOwn` checks only own enumerable-or-not properties, so it returns `false` even though `"role" in user` would return `true`.
`const` prevents reassigning the `config` binding itself, not mutation of the object it points to. Mutating a property is allowed.
`Array.prototype.sort` mutates the original array in place and returns the same reference, so `nums === sorted` is `true` and `nums` itself is now sorted, starting with `1`.
